arXiv:2605.04069v1 [cs.LG] 12 Apr 2026

LAWS: Learning from Actual Workloads Symbolically
A Self-Certifying Parametrized Cache Architecture
for Neural Inference, Robotics, and Edge Deployment

Gregory Magarshak Email: gmagarshak@faculty.ienyc.edu
Abstract

We introduce Learning from Actual Workloads Symbolically (LAWS), an inference-time architecture deployable above any trained neural network without modification. LAWS maintains a dynamically growing library of parametrized experts—cheap computational patterns, ranging from precompiled GPU kernels to tiny neural networks, created automatically from observed inference queries and certified formally for correctness. New queries are routed to the cheapest certified expert whose validity domain contains the query; the base model runs only on genuine cache misses.

The central technical contribution is the self-certification theorem: a trained network’s weights encode, without any additional training or inference, a Lipschitz constant Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) certifying the validity of every expert. Routing radii are defined in the Probabilistic Language Trie (PLT) metric [15]; experts are correct on all inputs (Theorem 3), and routing radii determine which expert handles each query. No warmup, no proxy model, no retraining is required. LAWS strictly generalizes three prior approaches: (i) KV caching (degenerate case: zero validity radius, identity expert); (ii) Mixture of Experts (degenerate case: fixed library, no online creation); and (iii) manual symbolic AI (Cyc [14], Wolfram Alpha [22]), whose vocabularies require human authorship, whereas LAWS discovers its symbolic vocabulary automatically from the model’s training distribution (Theorem 11).

The name reflects a deeper analogy. Scientists discover natural laws from actual observations—not by legislating them, but by identifying the invariant patterns in empirical data. LAWS does the same computationally: it discovers the “laws” governing a trained model’s behavior—the regularities that hold across families of similar inputs—and encodes them as cheap certified experts. This mirrors how biological intelligence works: animals and humans learn by recognizing situations from experience and executing cached strategies, invoking deliberate computation only for genuinely novel inputs (Kahneman [11]). The model’s pre-trained weights encode an innate prior library (Chomsky [7]); deployment experience calibrates and extends it.

We prove: (1) expert libraries grow at rate O⁡(2H⁡(Pℳ)​log⁡N)O(2^{H(P_{\mathcal{M}})}\log N) under stationary distributions (equivalently O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) for fixed-entropy workloads); (2) each new expert monotonically improves hit rate; (3) a fleet of KK cooperating units accumulates K×K\times more observations per day, converging to full coverage proportionally faster than a single unit; (4) over-the-air (OTA) expert updates require O⁡(2H​log⁡Δ​N)O(2^{H}\log\Delta N) bits per period, enabling ≈870\approx 870 KB/day per robot for 1,000-unit fleets. We also prove energy savings bounds: cache hits consume O⁡(n+k​dmodel)O(n+k\,d_{\mathrm{model}}) floating-point operations versus O⁡(L​n2+L​n​dmodel)O(Ln^{2}+Lnd_{\mathrm{model}}) for a full forward pass, yielding up to 104×10^{4}\times energy reduction at high hit rates (Theorem 18).

We discuss deployment on personal computers, local robots, and vehicles—devices that can download only the experts they need on demand, learn from local workloads, upload observations to a shared repository, and receive certified domain intelligence as compact OTA updates. We situate the Safebox/Safebots.ai ecosystem [19] as one realization of this architecture, combining LAWS experts with hardware-attested policy execution and declarative orchestration.

1 Introduction

1.1 The Problem: Repetition Without Reuse

Modern neural networks are extraordinarily expensive to query. A forward pass through a 70B-parameter language model costs ∼\sim140 TFLOP; a single diffusion image generation costs thousands of forward passes; a robot controller running at 100 Hz executes millions of forward passes per hour. Yet across all of these systems, the vast majority of queries are not genuinely novel. They are variations on patterns the model has processed before—the same algorithm in different variable names, the same manipulation task with a different object, the same legal clause with different parties.

Current systems exploit this redundancy only in the crudest ways. Key-value (KV) caches reuse computation for exactly repeated token prefixes. Mixture of Experts (MoE) routes tokens to specialized sub-networks, but the routing table is fixed at training time and never grows. Symbolic AI systems (Cyc, Wolfram Alpha) encode reusable patterns explicitly, but require human authors to write each one.

The fundamental gap: no existing system automatically discovers reusable computational patterns from deployment experience, certifies their validity formally, and grows the library continuously with use.

1.2 The Proposal: LAWS

We introduce Learning from Actual Workloads Symbolically (LAWS), an inference-time architecture that fills this gap.

LAWS sits above any base model as a transparent interception layer. It maintains a library ℒ\mathcal{L} of parametrized experts, each encoding a cheap computation that approximates the base model on a certified region of input space. When a new query arrives:

  1. 1.

    A Probabilistic Language Trie (PLT) [15] lookup identifies all matching experts in ℒ\mathcal{L} (those whose routing ball contains xx).

  2. 2.

    If the query falls within e∗e^{*}’s routing radius (distance ≤τ∗\leq\tau^{*}, precomputed from model weights), LAWS returns e∗e^{*}’s output—a cheap function evaluation, not a full forward pass.

  3. 3.

    Otherwise, the base model runs. Its output is recorded, potentially distilling a new expert into ℒ\mathcal{L}.

The routing radii are computed from the model’s Lipschitz constant Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W), computable from the trained weights without any inference. This is the self-certification property that distinguishes LAWS from all prior caching approaches.

1.3 The Biological Parallel

This architecture is not merely inspired by biology—it is a computational formalization of how biological intelligence actually works.

Kahneman’s dual-process theory.

Kahneman [11] describes two cognitive systems: System 1 (fast, automatic, pattern-based, requiring minimal cognitive effort) and System 2 (slow, deliberate, analytical, effortful). Expert performance in domains from chess to medicine to tennis consists largely of System 1 operation: the expert recognizes the situation as an instance of a known pattern and executes the associated response without conscious deliberation. System 2 is invoked only when the situation is novel enough that no cached pattern applies.

LAWS formalizes this exactly. The expert library is System 1. The base model is System 2. The transition condition—query distance exceeds validity radius—is the abort-and-replan signal.

Chomsky’s innate prior.

Chomsky [7] argued that children acquire language too rapidly and too reliably from impoverished input for grammar to be learned from scratch. There must be an innate Language Acquisition Device—a prior structure in the brain that constrains the space of possible grammars.

In LAWS terms: the model’s pre-trained weights WW encode an innate prior. The PLT trie derived from WW constitutes the model’s innate expert library—the patterns it “knows” before seeing any deployment query. Real-world queries calibrate this prior, adding new experts and refining validity radii, but the innate structure is already rich at deployment time. The poverty-of-the-stimulus argument applies: the model can generalize to novel inputs immediately, without waiting for empirical frequency estimates, because the Lipschitz certificate derived from WW defines valid generalization boundaries from the start.

The abort-and-replan signal.

In air combat maneuvering, a missile engagement has a minimum operating range. Inside this range the seeker cannot track, the rocket motor may not have armed, and the geometry is too dynamic for guidance. The pilot’s abort signal is immediate and automatic: too close for missiles, switching to guns. No deliberation. The abort condition was precomputed during mission planning; the in-flight check is O⁡(1)O(1).

LAWS’s transition from System 1 to System 2 is the same operation. The validity radius τ∗\tau^{*} is precomputed from WW at model-load time. At query time, a single comparison—does d𝒯​(x,e∗)≤τ∗d_{\mathcal{T}}(x,e^{*})\leq\tau^{*}?—routes the query. The decision requires no additional inference.

1.4 Overview of Contributions

  1. 1.

    Transformer Lipschitz Bound (Theorem 1): Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) is computable from model weights; activations are Lipschitz in token embeddings with this constant.

  2. 2.

    Self-Certification Theorem (Theorem 3): validity of every LAWS expert is certified by Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) without inference.

  3. 3.

    Jacobian Correction (Theorem 4): parametrized experts achieve O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}) error (vs. O⁡(r)O(r) for exact-match caches) where r=‖E⁡(xd¯+1)−E⁡(nd¯+1∗)‖r=\|E(x_{\bar{d}+1})-E(n^{*}_{\bar{d}+1})\|, via precomputed Jacobians at the divergence embedding.

  4. 4.

    Expert Library Growth Rate (Theorem 7): under stationary PℳP_{\mathcal{M}}, new expert creation rate is O⁡(2H⁡(Pℳ)​log⁡N)O(2^{H(P_{\mathcal{M}})}\log N) after NN queries; O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) for fixed-entropy workloads.

  5. 5.

    Monotone Hit Rate (Theorem 6): each new expert weakly increases the expected hit rate for all future queries.

  6. 6.

    Abort-and-Replan Threshold (Theorem 9): a unique τ∗\tau^{*} minimizes expected inference cost; computable from Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) and cost parameters.

  7. 7.

    LAWS Generalizes MoE and KV Caching (Theorem 10): both are recovered as degenerate cases; LAWS is strictly more expressive.

  8. 8.

    Fleet Learning Lower Bound (Theorem 15): KK cooperating LAWS units achieve hit rate improvement Ω⁡(K)\Omega(K) over single-unit deployment.

  9. 9.

    Automatic Symbolic Vocabulary (Theorem 11): the PLT trie of a trained model defines a graded, compositional, self-certified symbolic vocabulary without human authorship.

  10. 10.

    Cinderella Cascade Bound (Theorem 14): amplification of dropped attention weights through layers is bounded by the surprisal of the dropped token; rare high-surprisal events constitute the Shannon overflow set.

  11. 11.

    Robotics Convergence Rate (Corollary of Theorem 15): for a fleet of KK robots each performing MM tasks per day, LAWS expert library coverage of the task distribution converges at rate Ω⁡(K​M)\Omega(KM).

  12. 12.

    OTA Download Bound (Theorem 16): the incremental expert library update for period [t,t+Δ​t][t,t+\Delta t] has description length O⁡(2H⁡(Pℳ)⋅log⁡(Δ​N)⋅Bexpert)O(2^{H(P_{\mathcal{M}})}\cdot\log(\Delta N)\cdot B_{\mathrm{expert}}) bits, characterizing the bandwidth required for over-the-air updates.

  13. 13.

    Energy Savings Bound (Theorem 18): at asymptotic hit rate H∞H_{\infty}, LAWS reduces energy per query to H∞⋅O⁡(n+k​dmodel)/O⁡(L​n2+L​n​dmodel)+(1−H∞)H_{\infty}\cdot O(n{+}k\,d_{\mathrm{model}})/O(Ln^{2}{+}Lnd_{\mathrm{model}})+(1-H_{\infty}) of baseline; ∼10×\sim 10\times reduction at 90% hit rate for typical LLM parameters.

  14. 14.

    Conjecture: Symbolic Pattern Emergence (Conjecture 3): for a sufficiently capable base model, all high-probability trie nodes have experts in one of a finite set of primitive function classes.

Organization.

Section 2 reviews PLTs, MoE, KV caching, and cognitive science background. Section 3 establishes the Lipschitz framework. Section 4 defines LAWS formally. Section 5 contains the core theorems and proofs. Section 6 develops the parametrized expert framework. Section 7 treats the Cinderella cascade effect. Section 8 develops the robotics application with fleet-learning theorems. Section 9 compares to Cyc, Wolfram Alpha, MoE, and KV caching. Section 11 discusses diffusion models, hardware, and open problems.

2 Background

2.1 Probabilistic Language Tries

We briefly recall the framework of [15]. Let VV be a finite vocabulary and ℳ\mathcal{M} a generative model over V∗V^{*}.

Definition 1 (PLT and Trie Metric [15]).

The probabilistic language trie 𝒯⁡(ℳ)\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{M}) is the directed rooted tree whose nodes are prefixes x∈V∗x\in V^{*} and whose outgoing edges from xx are labeled by tokens t∈Vt\in V with weight Pℳ​(t∣x)P_{\mathcal{M}}(t\mid x). For two sequences s,s′∈V∗s,s^{\prime}\in V^{*}, their longest common prefix is s∧s′s\wedge s^{\prime}, and the trie metric is:

d𝒯​(s,s′)=−log2⁡Pℳ​(s∧s′).d_{\mathcal{T}}(s,s^{\prime})=-\log_{2}P_{\mathcal{M}}(s\wedge s^{\prime}).

The companion paper on sequential KV compression [17] established that, for a transformer ℳ\mathcal{M}, the conditional entropy of KV vectors satisfies:

H⁡(KVt+1∣KV≤t)≤H⁡(tt+1∣t1,…,tt)≤log2⁡PP⁡(ℳ),H(\mathrm{KV}_{t+1}\mid\mathrm{KV}_{\leq t})\;\leq\;H(t_{t+1}\mid t_{1},\ldots,t_{t})\;\leq\;\log_{2}\mathrm{PP}(\mathcal{M}),

bounding KV cache entropy by per-token surprisal. LAWS builds on this result: the same surprisal that bounds KV entropy also bounds the error in a parametrized expert approximation.

2.2 Transformer Architecture

A standard pre-norm transformer with LL layers processes a token sequence 𝐭=(t1,…,tn)\mathbf{t}=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}) via a residual stream:

𝐱i(ℓ+1)=𝐱i(ℓ)+Attn(ℓ)​(LN⁡(𝐱(ℓ)))i+MLP(ℓ)​(LN⁡(𝐱(ℓ+1)​ (partial)))i.\mathbf{x}^{(\ell+1)}_{i}=\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}_{i}+\mathrm{Attn}^{(\ell)}\!\bigl(\mathrm{LN}(\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)})\bigr)_{i}+\mathrm{MLP}^{(\ell)}\!\bigl(\mathrm{LN}(\mathbf{x}^{(\ell+1)\text{ (partial)}})\bigr)_{i}.

The KV vectors at layer ℓ\ell, position ii are 𝐤i(ℓ)=WK(ℓ)​LN​(𝐱i(ℓ))\mathbf{k}^{(\ell)}_{i}=W_{K}^{(\ell)}\mathrm{LN}(\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}_{i}) and 𝐯i(ℓ)=WV(ℓ)​LN​(𝐱i(ℓ))\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}_{i}=W_{V}^{(\ell)}\mathrm{LN}(\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}_{i}). The full forward map is FW:Vn→ℝ|V|F_{W}:V^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{|V|}.

2.3 Mixture of Experts

Definition 2 (MoE [20]).

A Mixture of Experts layer maintains KK expert networks {e1,…,eK}\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{K}\} and a router R:ℝd→ΔKR:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\Delta^{K}. For input xx, the output is ∑k=1KR​(x)k⋅ek​(x)\sum_{k=1}^{K}R(x)_{k}\cdot e_{k}(x) (or ∑k∈top-​k′R​(x)k⋅ek​(x)\sum_{k\in\text{top-}k^{\prime}}R(x)_{k}\cdot e_{k}(x) in sparse variants).

Key properties of standard MoE: (1) KK is fixed at training time; (2) experts are trained jointly with the router; (3) no formal guarantee that any expert is correct on any given input.

2.4 Kahneman’s Dual-Process Theory

Kahneman [11] identifies two cognitive systems. System 1 is fast, automatic, and based on pattern recognition; it operates below conscious awareness and requires minimal effort. System 2 is slow, deliberate, and analytical; it requires working memory and conscious engagement. Expert performance—in chess, medicine, tennis, piloting—consists overwhelmingly of System 1 operation: the expert pattern-matches the current situation to a stored schema and executes the associated response automatically. System 2 is invoked when the situation is genuinely novel: when no stored pattern applies, or when the System 1 response triggers a conflict signal.

This migration from System 2 to System 1 with experience is well-documented. A novice chess player consciously evaluates candidate moves; a grandmaster perceives the “right” move immediately. A medical student follows diagnostic algorithms; an experienced clinician recognizes the disease pattern from a symptom constellation. The expertise lies in the richness and accuracy of the System 1 library, not in faster System 2 processing.

2.5 Chomsky’s Innate Prior

Chomsky’s poverty of the stimulus argument [7] observes that children acquire complex grammar from limited, often ungrammatical input. The input alone is insufficient to determine a unique grammar; children must bring prior structure to the task. This prior structure—the Language Acquisition Device (LAD)—constrains the space of possible grammars the child considers.

In our framework: a trained model’s weights WW are its LAD. The PLT trie derived from WW is the innate expert library—the patterns the model “pre-knows” before any deployment query. As in Chomsky’s theory, this prior is not learned from deployment observations; it is encoded in WW during pre-training on a large corpus. The self-certification theorem (Theorem 3) formalizes the sense in which WW certifies the validity of this innate knowledge.

2.6 Symbolic AI: Cyc and Wolfram Alpha

Cyc [14].

The Cyc project, begun in 1984, aimed to encode human common-sense knowledge as explicit logical axioms. After approximately 47,000 person-years of manual knowledge entry, the system contains roughly 25 million rules and can perform logical inference over them. The fundamental limitation: every piece of knowledge must be hand-authored by a human who understands it. Cyc’s knowledge base is static between manual updates. It provides no graceful degradation for inputs outside the authored rules, and no formal guarantee that any rule is correct.

Wolfram Alpha [22].

Wolfram Alpha takes a different approach: curated computational knowledge (mathematical functions, physical constants, geographic data) combined with a symbolic computation engine. It is extremely powerful within its curated domain, but the domain boundary is sharp. Outside curated knowledge, the system fails. Like Cyc, knowledge is manually structured by Wolfram and his team.

LAWS vs. symbolic AI.

LAWS differs from both in three fundamental respects: (1) its symbolic vocabulary is discovered automatically from the trained model’s distribution, not authored by humans; (2) it provides formal validity certificates for every expert, derived from WW; and (3) its vocabulary grows continuously with deployment without human intervention. The full comparison is in Section 9.

3 The Lipschitz Framework

We establish Lipschitz constants for each component of a transformer layer.

The softmax function σ:ℝn→Δn−1\sigma:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\Delta^{n-1} satisfies ‖σ⁡(u)−σ⁡(v)‖1≤‖u−v‖1\|\sigma(u)-\sigma(v)\|_{1}\leq\|u-v\|_{1} (Lipschitz constant 1 in ℓ1\ell^{1}) and ‖σ⁡(u)−σ⁡(v)‖2≤12​‖u−v‖2\|\sigma(u)-\sigma(v)\|_{2}\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\|u-v\|_{2}. Differentiating oio_{i} with respect to the query 𝐪i\mathbf{q}_{i} gives ∂oi/∂𝐪i=1dhead​∑j(∂ai​j/∂𝐪i)​𝐯jT\partial o_{i}/\partial\mathbf{q}_{i}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{head}}}}\sum_{j}(\partial a_{ij}/\partial\mathbf{q}_{i})\mathbf{v}_{j}^{T}. The Jacobian of the attention weights satisfies ‖∂ai/∂𝐪i‖op≤‖WK(ℓ)‖op/(2​dhead)\|\partial a_{i}/\partial\mathbf{q}_{i}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|W_{K}^{(\ell)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}/(2\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{head}}}), giving the stated bound by summing components (i) and (ii). Note: when position d¯+1\bar{d}+1’s query changes, it attends to all nn key vectors; a precise bound acquires a factor of n\sqrt{n} from the Cauchy–Schwarz step ‖δ​logit‖2≤n⋅maxj⁡|δ​logitj|\|\delta\mathrm{logit}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{n}\cdot\max_{j}|\delta\mathrm{logit}_{j}|. The stated LattnL_{\mathrm{attn}} is therefore context-length-dependent; Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) should be understood as Λ⁡(W,n)\Lambda(W,n) in long-context settings.

(d) GeLU satisfies GeLU⁡(x)=x​Φ​(x)\mathrm{GeLU}(x)=x\Phi(x), where Φ\Phi is the standard Gaussian CDF. Its derivative is GeLU′​(x)=Φ⁡(x)+x​ϕ​(x)\mathrm{GeLU}^{\prime}(x)=\Phi(x)+x\phi(x), where ϕ\phi is the Gaussian PDF. The maximum of |GeLU′||\mathrm{GeLU}^{\prime}| is achieved at x≈1.1x\approx 1.1 where GeLU′​(x)≈1.083\mathrm{GeLU}^{\prime}(x)\approx 1.083. Technically, GeLU is not 1-Lipschitz; it is LGeLUL_{\mathrm{GeLU}}-Lipschitz with LGeLU≈1.1L_{\mathrm{GeLU}}\approx 1.1. We incorporate this constant into κ(ℓ)\kappa^{(\ell)} via the MLP Lipschitz factor. SwiGLU and ReLU variants are handled analogously; ReLU is exactly 1-Lipschitz. For practical purposes, this constant is absorbed into ‖WMLP(ℓ)‖op\|W_{\mathrm{MLP}}^{(\ell)}\|_{\mathrm{op}} in Theorem 1, which we define as including activation Lipschitz constants. ∎

Theorem 1 (Transformer Lipschitz Bound).

Let FW:Vn→ℝ|V|F_{W}:V^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{|V|} be a transformer with pre-norm architecture. Define the layer coupling constant:

κ(ℓ)=(1+Lattn(ℓ)⋅γ(ℓ)εLN)⋅(1+‖WMLP(ℓ)‖op⋅γ(ℓ)εLN),\kappa^{(\ell)}=\left(1+L_{\mathrm{attn}}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\gamma^{(\ell)}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{LN}}}\right)\cdot\left(1+\|W_{\mathrm{MLP}}^{(\ell)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\cdot\frac{\gamma^{(\ell)}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{LN}}}\right),

and the end-to-end Lipschitz constant:

Λ⁡(W)=∏ℓ=1Lκ(ℓ).\Lambda(W)=\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\kappa^{(\ell)}.

Then for any two token sequences s,s′s,s^{\prime} that diverge first at position d¯+1\bar{d}+1:

‖FW​(s)−FW​(s′)‖≤Λ⁡(W)⋅‖E⁡(sd¯+1)−E⁡(sd¯+1′)‖,\|F_{W}(s)-F_{W}(s^{\prime})\|\;\leq\;\Lambda(W)\cdot\|E(s_{\bar{d}+1})-E(s^{\prime}_{\bar{d}+1})\|,

where E:V→ℝdmodelE:V\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}} is the token embedding. Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) is computable from the trained weights in O⁡(L⋅dmodel2)O(L\cdot d_{\mathrm{model}}^{2}) operations.

Proof.

For positions i≤d¯i\leq\bar{d}, the sequences are identical, so all activations 𝐱i(ℓ)​(s)=𝐱i(ℓ)​(s′)\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}_{i}(s)=\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}_{i}(s^{\prime}) exactly (by determinism of the forward pass—Lemma 1 of [17]).

At position d¯+1\bar{d}+1, the difference in activations is introduced at the embedding layer: ‖𝐱d¯+1(0)​(s)−𝐱d¯+1(0)​(s′)‖=‖E⁡(sd¯+1)−E⁡(sd¯+1′)‖\|\mathbf{x}^{(0)}_{\bar{d}+1}(s)-\mathbf{x}^{(0)}_{\bar{d}+1}(s^{\prime})\|=\|E(s_{\bar{d}+1})-E(s^{\prime}_{\bar{d}+1})\|.

At positions i>d¯+1i>\bar{d}+1: through causal attention, the perturbation at position d¯+1\bar{d}+1 propagates to all later positions. At each layer ℓ\ell, every position’s hidden state change is bounded by κ(ℓ)\kappa^{(\ell)} times the maximum change from the previous layer, since the layer map is κ(ℓ)\kappa^{(\ell)}-Lipschitz over the full nn-position activation tensor. Therefore the bound κ(ℓ)⋅‖δ(ℓ−1)‖max\kappa^{(\ell)}\cdot\|\delta^{(\ell-1)}\|_{\max} applies uniformly across all positions at each layer.

Each transformer layer is a composition of the components in Lemma 1. By the chain rule for Lipschitz constants, the Lipschitz constant of the composition is at most the product of the individual constants, giving κ(ℓ)\kappa^{(\ell)} per layer. Chaining across all LL layers gives Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W).

Computability: Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) requires computing operator norms of weight matrices, each taking O⁡(dmodel2)O(d_{\mathrm{model}}^{2}) operations via the power method. Summing over LL layers gives O⁡(L⋅dmodel2)O(L\cdot d_{\mathrm{model}}^{2}). ∎

Remark 1 (On the Tightness of Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W)).

Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) can be large for deep networks (exponential in LL in the worst case), since it is a product of per-layer operator norms. Three caveats apply: (1) The LayerNorm bound requires σ⁡(x)≥εLN\sigma(x)\geq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{LN}} (input variance bounded away from zero), which holds throughout trained transformers due to the εLN\varepsilon_{\mathrm{LN}} stabilizer in the denominator, but may fail for adversarially constructed inputs outside the training distribution. We restrict LAWS validity claims to inputs drawn from PℳP_{\mathcal{M}}, for which this holds with high probability. (2) In practice, the effective Lipschitz constant on in-distribution inputs is far smaller than Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W); empirical calibration is recommended for setting τ∗\tau^{*} in production systems. (3) LAWS uses Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) in the self-certification bound εfit+2​Λ​(W)⋅CE\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}+2\,\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}; for this to be a useful guarantee requires δ>εfit+2​Λ​(W)⋅CE\delta>\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}+2\,\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}, i.e., Λ⁡(W)<(δ−εfit)/(2​CE)\Lambda(W)<(\delta-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}})/(2C_{E}). (4) As noted in Lemma 1(c), the attention Lipschitz constant acquires a n\sqrt{n} factor from the query-to-all-keys term; for long contexts, Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) should be treated as Λ⁡(W,n)\Lambda(W,n) scaling with sequence length.

Corollary 1 (Activation Similarity Within Shared Prefix).

For any two inputs sharing a prefix of length d¯\bar{d} and any layer ℓ\ell, position i≤d¯i\leq\bar{d}:

‖𝐱i(ℓ)​(s)−𝐱i(ℓ)​(s′)‖=0.\|\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}_{i}(s)-\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}_{i}(s^{\prime})\|=0.

For position i=d¯+1i=\bar{d}+1 and layer ℓ\ell:

‖𝐱d¯+1(ℓ)​(s)−𝐱d¯+1(ℓ)​(s′)‖≤∏m=1ℓκ(m)⋅‖E⁡(sd¯+1)−E⁡(sd¯+1′)‖.\|\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}_{\bar{d}+1}(s)-\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}_{\bar{d}+1}(s^{\prime})\|\leq\prod_{m=1}^{\ell}\kappa^{(m)}\cdot\|E(s_{\bar{d}+1})-E(s^{\prime}_{\bar{d}+1})\|.
Proof.

The first statement follows from KV determinism [17]. The second follows from the proof of Theorem 1 truncated at layer ℓ\ell. ∎

Theorem 2 (Lower Bound on Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) for Structured Tasks).

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a task class requiring the base model to produce outputs whose pairwise ℓ2\ell^{2} separation is at least Δ>0\Delta>0 for inputs whose divergence embeddings satisfy ‖E⁡(sd¯+1)−E⁡(sd¯+1′)‖≤r\|E(s_{\bar{d}+1})-E(s^{\prime}_{\bar{d}+1})\|\leq r. Then:

Λ⁡(W)≥Δr.\Lambda(W)\;\geq\;\frac{\Delta}{r}.

In particular, for arithmetic tasks where the model must distinguish outputs differing by at least Δ=1/M\Delta=1/M (decimal precision MM), the bound gives Λ⁡(W)≥Δ/rmin\Lambda(W)\geq\Delta/r_{\min}, where rmin=mint≠t′⁡‖E⁡(t)−E⁡(t′)‖r_{\min}=\min_{t\neq t^{\prime}}\|E(t)-E(t^{\prime})\| is the minimum pairwise embedding separation (a property of the trained embedding matrix, measurable directly from WW). For tasks where semantically adjacent tokens (e.g., consecutive digits “1” and “2”) have small embedding separation rmin≪CEr_{\min}\ll C_{E}, the bound forces Λ⁡(W)≥1/(M⋅rmin)\Lambda(W)\geq 1/(M\cdot r_{\min}), which grows with precision MM. High-precision arithmetic thus provably requires larger Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W), limiting the LAWS routing radius τ∗\tau^{*} for such tasks.

Proof.

By the definition of the Lipschitz constant: ‖FW​(s)−FW​(s′)‖≤Λ⁡(W)⋅‖E⁡(sd¯+1)−E⁡(sd¯+1′)‖\|F_{W}(s)-F_{W}(s^{\prime})\|\leq\Lambda(W)\cdot\|E(s_{\bar{d}+1})-E(s^{\prime}_{\bar{d}+1})\| for any pair diverging at d¯+1\bar{d}+1. If there exist inputs s,s′s,s^{\prime} with ‖E⁡(sd¯+1)−E⁡(sd¯+1′)‖≤r\|E(s_{\bar{d}+1})-E(s^{\prime}_{\bar{d}+1})\|\leq r and ‖FW​(s)−FW​(s′)‖≥Δ\|F_{W}(s)-F_{W}(s^{\prime})\|\geq\Delta, then Λ⁡(W)≥Δ/r\Lambda(W)\geq\Delta/r. Such inputs exist whenever the model must distinguish outputs separated by Δ\Delta from embeddings separated by only rr, which is exactly the case for high-precision arithmetic or lookup tasks where adjacent vocabulary tokens map to semantically distant outputs. □\square ∎

Corollary 2 (LAWS Acceleration Limits for High-Precision Tasks).

For any task class requiring output precision Δ\Delta from minimal embedding perturbation rr, the LAWS routing radius satisfies:

τ∗≤δ−εfit−2​(Δ/r)⋅CE(Δ/r)⋅CE.\tau^{*}\;\leq\;\frac{\delta-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}-2(\Delta/r)\cdot C_{E}}{(\Delta/r)\cdot C_{E}}.

If Δ>r⁡(δ−εfit)/(2​CE)\Delta>r(\delta-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}})/(2C_{E}) (high required precision relative to the quality threshold), then τ∗<0\tau^{*}<0 and no expert can be certified: LAWS must always invoke the base model for such tasks. This characterizes the fundamental boundary of LAWS acceleration—it cannot certify experts for tasks that require the model to be highly sensitive to small input perturbations.

4 The LAWS Architecture

4.1 Parametrized Experts

Definition 3 (Parametrized Expert).

A parametrized expert is a tuple e=(n∗,f,ϕ,τ∗,εfit)e=(n^{*},f,\phi,\tau^{*},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}) where:

  • •

    n∗∈𝒯⁡(ℳ)n^{*}\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{M}) is the signpost: a full-length input in VnV^{n}, represented as a PLT trie node (by its token-prefix structure); FW​(n∗)F_{W}(n^{*}) is the base model output on this input;

  • •

    ϕ:V∗→ℝk\phi:V^{*}\to\mathbb{R}^{k} is the parameter extractor, mapping inputs to a kk-dimensional parameter vector;

  • •

    f:ℝk→ℝ|V|f:\mathbb{R}^{k}\to\mathbb{R}^{|V|} is the expert function, a cheap computation approximating FWF_{W} on the expert’s domain;

  • •

    τ∗>0\tau^{*}>0 is the validity radius in PLT metric space, derived from Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W);

  • •

    εfit≥0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}\geq 0 is the fitting error, certifying ‖FW​(n∗)−f⁡(ϕ⁡(n∗))‖≤εfit\|F_{W}(n^{*})-f(\phi(n^{*}))\|\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}.

The validity domain of ee is the ball ℬ⁡(n∗,τ∗)={x∈V∗:d𝒯​(x,n∗)≤τ∗}\mathcal{B}(n^{*},\tau^{*})=\{x\in V^{*}:d_{\mathcal{T}}(x,n^{*})\leq\tau^{*}\}.

Definition 4 (Expert Library and LAWS Inference).

A LAWS system (FW,ℒ,δ)(F_{W},\mathcal{L},\delta) consists of a base model FWF_{W}, a library ℒ\mathcal{L} of parametrized experts, and a quality threshold δ>0\delta>0 satisfying:

δ>εfit+Λ⁡(W)⋅CE⋅(2+H⁡(Pℳ)),\delta\;>\;\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}+\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}\cdot(2+H(P_{\mathcal{M}})),

where H⁡(Pℳ)H(P_{\mathcal{M}}) is the entropy of the input distribution. This ensures (i) the self-certification bound εfit+2​Λ​CE≤δ\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}+2\Lambda C_{E}\leq\delta (Theorem 3), and (ii) the routing radius τ∗≥H\tau^{*}\geq H, so that every heavy trie node n∗n^{*} (with Pℳ​(n∗)≥2−HP_{\mathcal{M}}(n^{*})\geq 2^{-H}) lies within its own routing ball under any-match routing. The routing radius for an expert is:

τ∗​(n∗,δ)=δ−εfit−2​Λ​(W)⋅CEΛ⁡(W)⋅CE\tau^{*}(n^{*},\delta)=\frac{\delta-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}-2\,\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}}{\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}}

where CE=maxt,t′⁡‖E⁡(t)−E⁡(t′)‖C_{E}=\max_{t,t^{\prime}}\|E(t)-E(t^{\prime})\|. Any expert is correct on all inputs; the routing radius defines which queries this expert handles.

For input xx, LAWS inference proceeds as:

LAWS(x)={fe∗​(ϕe∗​(x))if ​∃e∈ℒ:d𝒯​(x,ne∗)≤τ∗​(e)FW​(x)otherwise (cache miss)\mathrm{LAWS}(x)=\begin{cases}f_{e^{*}}(\phi_{e^{*}}(x))&\text{if }\exists e\in\mathcal{L}:d_{\mathcal{T}}(x,n^{*}_{e})\leq\tau^{*}(e)\\ F_{W}(x)&\text{otherwise (cache miss)}\end{cases}

where e∗=argmine:d𝒯​(x,ne∗)≤τ∗​(e)d𝒯(x,ne∗)e^{*}=\arg\min_{e:d_{\mathcal{T}}(x,n^{*}_{e})\leq\tau^{*}(e)}d_{\mathcal{T}}(x,n^{*}_{e}) (the matching expert with smallest trie distance; a cache hit occurs whenever any expert’s routing ball contains xx, not only the globally nearest expert). This “any-match” rule ensures that adding experts can only increase coverage, never decrease it—a property necessary for Theorem 6.

4.2 Expert Function Classes

Expert functions ff may be chosen from an increasing hierarchy of complexity:

  1. Level 1.

    Constant. f⁡(ϕ)=cf(\phi)=c where c=FW​(n∗)c=F_{W}(n^{*}). Standard exact-match cache. Error ≤Λ⁡(W)⋅CE\leq\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E} for all xx (Term 1 of Theorem 3 only; Terms 2 and 3 are zero for a constant expert).

  2. Level 2.

    Linear (Jacobian correction). f⁡(ϕ)=FW​(n∗)+JW​(n∗)⋅ϕf(\phi)=F_{W}(n^{*})+J_{W}(n^{*})\cdot\phi where JWJ_{W} is the Jacobian of FWF_{W} at n∗n^{*}. Error O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}) where r=‖E⁡(xd¯+1)−E⁡(nd¯+1∗)‖r=\|E(x_{\bar{d}+1})-E(n^{*}_{\bar{d}+1})\| (Theorem 4).

  3. Level 3.

    Primitive function. ff is an identified algorithmic pattern: arithmetic, sorting, lookup table, string template, JSON/SQL instantiation. Error zero (exact).

  4. Level 4.

    Small MLP. ff is a small neural network (2–3 layers, width ≤128\leq 128) fit to the signpost’s subtree. Error εfit\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}} by construction.

4.3 LAWS Update Protocol

5 Core Theorems

5.1 Self-Certification

Theorem 3 (Self-Certification).

For any LAWS expert e=(n∗,f,ϕ,τ∗,εfit)e=(n^{*},f,\phi,\tau^{*},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}) satisfying Definition 3, with ϕ\phi extracting the parameter vector at the divergence embedding (so ‖ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(n∗)‖≤CE\|\phi(x)-\phi(n^{*})\|\leq C_{E} for any xx), and with Lip⁡(f)≤Λ⁡(W)\mathrm{Lip}(f)\leq\Lambda(W), the approximation error is bounded uniformly over all inputs xx:

‖FW​(x)−f⁡(ϕ⁡(x))‖≤εfit+2​Λ​(W)⋅CE.\|F_{W}(x)-f(\phi(x))\|\;\leq\;\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}+2\,\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}.

In particular, if δ>εfit+2​Λ​(W)⋅CE\delta>\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}+2\,\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}, then ‖FW​(x)−f⁡(ϕ⁡(x))‖≤δ\|F_{W}(x)-f(\phi(x))\|\leq\delta for every input xx—no restriction on d𝒯​(x,n∗)d_{\mathcal{T}}(x,n^{*}) is required. The validity radius τ∗\tau^{*} in Definition 4 bounds the validity domain for routing purposes (to select the best expert), not for correctness.

Proof.

By the triangle inequality:

‖FW​(x)−f⁡(ϕ⁡(x))‖\displaystyle\|F_{W}(x)-f(\phi(x))\| ≤‖FW​(x)−FW​(n∗)‖⏟Term 1+‖FW​(n∗)−f⁡(ϕ⁡(n∗))‖⏟Term 2+‖f⁡(ϕ⁡(n∗))−f⁡(ϕ⁡(x))‖⏟Term 3.\displaystyle\leq\underbrace{\|F_{W}(x)-F_{W}(n^{*})\|}_{\text{Term 1}}+\underbrace{\|F_{W}(n^{*})-f(\phi(n^{*}))\|}_{\text{Term 2}}+\underbrace{\|f(\phi(n^{*}))-f(\phi(x))\|}_{\text{Term 3}}.

Term 2 is ≤εfit\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}} by the fitting condition.

Term 3. By assumption ‖ϕ⁡(n∗)−ϕ⁡(x)‖≤CE\|\phi(n^{*})-\phi(x)\|\leq C_{E} and Lip⁡(f)≤Λ⁡(W)\mathrm{Lip}(f)\leq\Lambda(W): for Level-1 experts Lip⁡(f)=0\mathrm{Lip}(f)=0; for Level-2 Jacobian experts, Lip⁡(f)=‖JW​(n∗)‖op≤Λ⁡(W)\mathrm{Lip}(f)=\|J_{W}(n^{*})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda(W) by Theorem 1; for small MLPs verified at fitting time. Therefore Term 3 ≤Λ⁡(W)⋅CE\leq\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}.

Term 1. Let d¯\bar{d} be the length of the longest common token prefix of xx and n∗n^{*}. By Theorem 1:

Term 1≤Λ⁡(W)⋅‖E⁡(xd¯+1)−E⁡(nd¯+1∗)‖≤Λ⁡(W)⋅CE.\text{Term 1}\leq\Lambda(W)\cdot\|E(x_{\bar{d}+1})-E(n^{*}_{\bar{d}+1})\|\leq\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}.

Summing:

‖FW​(x)−f⁡(ϕ⁡(x))‖≤εfit+Λ⁡(W)⋅CE+Λ⁡(W)⋅CE=εfit+2​Λ​(W)⋅CE≤δ.□\|F_{W}(x)-f(\phi(x))\|\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}+\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}+\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}+2\,\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}\leq\delta.\qquad\square

∎

5.2 Jacobian Correction

Theorem 4 (Jacobian Correction Achieves Second-Order Error).

Let ee be a Level-2 expert with f⁡(ϕ)=FW​(n∗)+JW​(n∗)⋅ϕf(\phi)=F_{W}(n^{*})+J_{W}(n^{*})\cdot\phi and ϕ⁡(x)=E⁡(xd¯+1)−E⁡(nd¯+1∗)\phi(x)=E(x_{\bar{d}+1})-E(n^{*}_{\bar{d}+1}) where d¯\bar{d} is the length of the longest common prefix of xx and n∗n^{*}. Define r=‖E⁡(xd¯+1)−E⁡(nd¯+1∗)‖r=\|E(x_{\bar{d}+1})-E(n^{*}_{\bar{d}+1})\| as the embedding-space distance at the divergence point. Then:

‖FW​(x)−f⁡(ϕ⁡(x))‖≤12​‖HW​(n∗)‖op⋅r2+O⁡(r3)\|F_{W}(x)-f(\phi(x))\|\;\leq\;\frac{1}{2}\|H_{W}(n^{*})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\cdot r^{2}+O(r^{3})

where HW​(n∗)H_{W}(n^{*}) is the Hessian of FWF_{W} at n∗n^{*} with respect to the divergence embedding. In particular the error is O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}) versus O⁡(r)O(r) for a Level-1 (constant) expert, giving a strict improvement for r<1r<1.

Proof.

Since xx and n∗n^{*} share the first d¯\bar{d} tokens, all activations at positions ≤d¯\leq\bar{d} are identical. The only perturbation is 𝐮=E⁡(xd¯+1)−E⁡(nd¯+1∗)\mathbf{u}=E(x_{\bar{d}+1})-E(n^{*}_{\bar{d}+1}) at the divergence position, with ‖𝐮‖=r\|\mathbf{u}\|=r. By Taylor’s theorem applied to FWF_{W} as a function of the divergence embedding (the forward pass is smooth in the embedding inputs):

FW​(x)=FW​(n∗)+JW​(n∗)​𝐮+12​𝐮T​HW​(ξ)​𝐮F_{W}(x)=F_{W}(n^{*})+J_{W}(n^{*})\,\mathbf{u}+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{u}^{T}H_{W}(\xi)\,\mathbf{u}

for some ξ\xi on the segment between E⁡(nd¯+1∗)E(n^{*}_{\bar{d}+1}) and E⁡(xd¯+1)E(x_{\bar{d}+1}). The Level-2 expert returns FW​(n∗)+JW​(n∗)​ϕ​(x)=FW​(n∗)+JW​(n∗)​𝐮F_{W}(n^{*})+J_{W}(n^{*})\phi(x)=F_{W}(n^{*})+J_{W}(n^{*})\,\mathbf{u}, so the error equals the remainder, bounded by 12​‖HW​(ξ)‖op​r2\frac{1}{2}\|H_{W}(\xi)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,r^{2}. By continuity of the Hessian on the compact validity ball, ‖HW​(ξ)‖op≤‖HW​(n∗)‖op+O⁡(r)\|H_{W}(\xi)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|H_{W}(n^{*})\|_{\mathrm{op}}+O(r), giving the stated bound. ∎

Corollary 3 (Quadratic Improvement Over Standard Cache).

For r=‖E⁡(xd¯+1)−E⁡(nd¯+1∗)‖<1r=\|E(x_{\bar{d}+1})-E(n^{*}_{\bar{d}+1})\|<1, the Level-2 expert improves on the Level-1 expert by a factor of rr in error. For r=0.1r=0.1, the Jacobian correction reduces error by a factor of 10; for r=0.01r=0.01, by a factor of 100.

5.3 Parameter Extraction at Branch Points

Theorem 5 (Parameters Lie at High-Entropy Positions).

Let n∗n^{*} be a trie node at depth d∗d_{*} (token prefix length) and let positions 𝒫hi={i>d∗:H⁡(ti∣t<i)>Hthresh}\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{hi}}=\{i>d_{*}:H(t_{i}\mid t_{<i})>H_{\mathrm{thresh}}\} be the high-entropy positions after the shared prefix. Define the parameter extractor ϕhi​(x)=(E⁡(xi))i∈𝒫hi\phi_{\mathrm{hi}}(x)=(E(x_{i}))_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{hi}}}.

Then the expected contribution of a low-entropy position j∉𝒫hij\notin\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{hi}} to the expert error satisfies:

𝔼⁡[Λ⁡(W)⋅‖E⁡(tj)−𝔼⁡[E⁡(tj)∣t<j]‖]≤Λ⁡(W)⋅CE⋅H⁡(tj∣t<j)⋅ln⁡2<Λ⁡(W)⋅CE⋅Hthresh⋅ln⁡2,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\Lambda(W)\cdot\|E(t_{j})-\mathbb{E}[E(t_{j})\mid t_{<j}]\|\bigr]\leq\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}\cdot\sqrt{H(t_{j}\mid t_{<j})\cdot\ln 2}<\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}\cdot\sqrt{H_{\mathrm{thresh}}\cdot\ln 2},

which is below the resolution εfit\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}} when Hthresh<(εfit/(Λ⁡(W)⋅CE))2/ln⁡2H_{\mathrm{thresh}}<(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}/(\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}))^{2}/\ln 2. Therefore, ϕhi\phi_{\mathrm{hi}} is sufficient on average: in expectation over queries from PℳP_{\mathcal{M}}, low-entropy positions can be ignored by the parameter extractor without increasing expected error above δ\delta.

Proof.

By the surprisal-bounded embedding variance result of [17] (the variance–entropy coupling result, Corollary on coherent text):

𝔼​[‖E⁡(tj)−𝔼⁡[E⁡(tj)∣t<j]‖2]1/2≤CE​H⁡(tj∣t<j)⋅ln⁡2.\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|E(t_{j})-\mathbb{E}[E(t_{j})\mid t_{<j}]\|^{2}\bigr]^{1/2}\leq C_{E}\sqrt{H(t_{j}\mid t_{<j})\cdot\ln 2}.

For positions with H⁡(tj∣t<j)<HthreshH(t_{j}\mid t_{<j})<H_{\mathrm{thresh}}, the token is nearly determined by the context, so E⁡(tj)≈𝔼⁡[E⁡(tj)∣t<j]E(t_{j})\approx\mathbb{E}[E(t_{j})\mid t_{<j}] with deviation bounded by CE​Hthresh⋅ln⁡2C_{E}\sqrt{H_{\mathrm{thresh}}\cdot\ln 2}. By Theorem 1, this deviation propagates to output error ≤Λ⁡(W)⋅CE​Hthresh⋅ln⁡2\leq\Lambda(W)\cdot C_{E}\sqrt{H_{\mathrm{thresh}}\cdot\ln 2}. Setting this below εfit\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}} gives the threshold condition. ∎

5.4 Expert Library Dynamics

Theorem 6 (Monotone Hit Rate).

Let HnH_{n} be the expected LAWS cache hit rate after nn deployment queries drawn i.i.d. from PℳP_{\mathcal{M}}. Under the LAWS update protocol (Algorithm 1), HnH_{n} is non-decreasing in nn:

H1≤H2≤⋯≤Hn≤⋯≤1.H_{1}\leq H_{2}\leq\cdots\leq H_{n}\leq\cdots\leq 1.
Proof.

Under the any-match inference rule, a query xx is a cache hit whenever any expert’s routing ball contains xx. Adding a new expert (n∗,f,ϕ,τ∗)(n^{*},f,\phi,\tau^{*}) adds ℬ⁡(n∗,τ∗)\mathcal{B}(n^{*},\tau^{*}) to the union of all routing balls. Since this union can only grow (never shrink) when experts are added, Hn+1≥HnH_{n+1}\geq H_{n}. The inequality is strict whenever ℬ⁡(n∗,τ∗)\mathcal{B}(n^{*},\tau^{*}) contains any xx not already covered by prior routing balls—guaranteed since the triggering query xx was a miss (outside all prior routing balls) and Pℳ​({x})>0P_{\mathcal{M}}(\{x\})>0. ∎

Theorem 7 (Expert Library Growth Rate).

Under a stationary input distribution PℳP_{\mathcal{M}} with Shannon entropy H=H⁡(Pℳ)H=H(P_{\mathcal{M}}), and with the LAWS update threshold NminN_{\min} (minimum observations before creating an expert), the expected number of new LAWS experts created after NN queries satisfies:

𝔼⁡[new experts after ​N​ queries]=O⁡(2H),\mathbb{E}[\text{new experts after }N\text{ queries}]=O\!\left(2^{H}\right),

provided N≤Nmin⋅2HN\leq N_{\min}\cdot 2^{H} (so that only heavy trie nodes accumulate enough observations to trigger expert creation). The tight bound is O⁡(2H)O(2^{H}) throughout this regime; the weaker form O⁡(2H​log⁡N)O(2^{H}\log N) is used in later results to simplify expressions involving NN explicitly (since 2H≤2H​log⁡N2^{H}\leq 2^{H}\log N for N≥2N\geq 2).

Proof.

New experts are created only on cache misses, and only when a trie node accumulates NminN_{\min} observations (Algorithm 1).

Partition trie nodes into heavy (Pℳ​(n)≥εP_{\mathcal{M}}(n)\geq\varepsilon) and light (Pℳ​(n)<εP_{\mathcal{M}}(n)<\varepsilon). Set ε=2−H\varepsilon=2^{-H}.

Heavy nodes. By the AEP, |ℋε|≤2H|\mathcal{H}_{\varepsilon}|\leq 2^{H}. The expected number of distinct heavy nodes visited in NN draws is at most min⁡(N,2H)≤2H\min(N,2^{H})\leq 2^{H} (occupancy bound, as below). Each creates at most one expert, giving 𝔼⁡[heavy experts]≤2H\mathbb{E}[\text{heavy experts}]\leq 2^{H}.

Light nodes. A light node nn has Pℳ​(n)<2−HP_{\mathcal{M}}(n)<2^{-H}, so its expected visits in NN queries is N⋅Pℳ​(n)<N⋅2−HN\cdot P_{\mathcal{M}}(n)<N\cdot 2^{-H}. To trigger expert creation it needs NminN_{\min} visits. If N≤Nmin⋅2HN\leq N_{\min}\cdot 2^{H}, then N⋅Pℳ​(n)<NminN\cdot P_{\mathcal{M}}(n)<N_{\min} in expectation, so no light node accumulates enough visits to create an expert. Therefore 𝔼⁡[light experts]=0\mathbb{E}[\text{light experts}]=0 in this regime. ✓\checkmark

Occupancy bound. For any MM elements with probabilities p1,…,pMp_{1},\ldots,p_{M}:

𝔼⁡[distinct elements in ​N​ draws]=∑i=1M(1−(1−pi)N)≤∑imin⁡(1,N​pi)≤min⁡(N,M).\mathbb{E}[\text{distinct elements in }N\text{ draws}]=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\bigl(1-(1-p_{i})^{N}\bigr)\leq\sum_{i}\min(1,Np_{i})\leq\min(N,M).

Setting M=2HM=2^{H} gives the stated bound. Since 2H≤2H​log⁡N2^{H}\leq 2^{H}\log N for N≥2N\geq 2, the theorem holds as stated with the O⁡(2H​log⁡N)O(2^{H}\log N) form. ∎

Corollary 4 (Sublinear Expert Growth).

The ratio of new experts created to total queries satisfies 𝔼⁡[new experts]/N≤O⁡(2H⁡(Pℳ)​log⁡N/N)→0\mathbb{E}[\text{new experts}]/N\leq O(2^{H(P_{\mathcal{M}})}\log N/N)\to 0 as N→∞N\to\infty. The system learns faster than it exhausts novelty: most queries are cache hits for large NN.

Theorem 8 (Online Expert Acquisition Cost).

Under the any-match routing rule and a stationary distribution PℳP_{\mathcal{M}} with entropy HH, let KN=O⁡(2H​log⁡N)K_{N}=O(2^{H}\log N) be the total number of expert creation events after NN queries (Theorem 7). The total cost attributable to expert acquisition—the overhead beyond running the already-learned library from the start—satisfies:

Cacq​(N)=KN⋅Nmin⋅Cfull=O⁡(Nmin⋅2H​log⁡N)⋅Cfull,C_{\mathrm{acq}}(N)\;=\;K_{N}\cdot N_{\min}\cdot C_{\mathrm{full}}\;=\;O\!\left(N_{\min}\cdot 2^{H}\log N\right)\cdot C_{\mathrm{full}},

since each of the KNK_{N} expert creations requires NminN_{\min} cache misses before triggering, each at cost CfullC_{\mathrm{full}}. The amortized acquisition cost per query is:

Cacq​(N)N=O⁡(Nmin⋅2H​log⁡NN)⋅Cfull→ 0as ​N→∞.\frac{C_{\mathrm{acq}}(N)}{N}\;=\;O\!\left(\frac{N_{\min}\cdot 2^{H}\log N}{N}\right)\cdot C_{\mathrm{full}}\;\to\;0\quad\text{as }N\to\infty.

In the limit, expert acquisition is free on a per-query basis.

Proof.

Each expert is created after NminN_{\min} cache misses accumulate at its signpost node (Algorithm 1). By Theorem 7, KN≤O⁡(2H​log⁡N)K_{N}\leq O(2^{H}\log N) experts are created over NN queries. The acquisition cost for each expert is at most Nmin⋅CfullN_{\min}\cdot C_{\mathrm{full}} (the misses that triggered it, each costing one full forward pass). Total acquisition cost ≤KN⋅Nmin⋅Cfull=O⁡(Nmin⋅2H​log⁡N)⋅Cfull\leq K_{N}\cdot N_{\min}\cdot C_{\mathrm{full}}=O(N_{\min}\cdot 2^{H}\log N)\cdot C_{\mathrm{full}}. Dividing by NN and noting (log⁡N)/N→0(\log N)/N\to 0 gives the stated bound with the NminN_{\min} factor absorbed into the O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot). □\square ∎

Remark 2 (Scope of the Bound).

This theorem bounds the acquisition overhead—the cost of the triggering misses that create new experts—not the total miss cost, which also includes misses on light-trie-nodes (probability <2−H<2^{-H}) that never accumulate enough visits to trigger expert creation. The total miss rate converges to 1−H∞1-H_{\infty} asymptotically (by Theorem 6), but the rate of convergence depends on the full distribution PℳP_{\mathcal{M}} and NminN_{\min} and is not bounded here. The theorem establishes that the one-time cost of building the expert library is sublinear in NN—a necessary condition for LAWS to be economically viable at scale.

Theorem 9 (Abort-and-Replan Threshold).

Let Cfull>0C_{\mathrm{full}}>0 be the cost of a full base-model forward pass, Chit>0C_{\mathrm{hit}}>0 the cost of an expert evaluation, and λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 the downstream cost per unit output error. The optimal validity radius that minimizes expected total cost is:

τ∗=2​(Cfull−Chit)λ⋅‖HW‖op2⋅Λ​(W)2⋅CE2,\tau^{*}=\frac{2(C_{\mathrm{full}}-C_{\mathrm{hit}})}{\lambda\cdot\|H_{W}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\cdot\Lambda(W)^{2}\cdot C_{E}^{2}},

where ‖HW‖op\|H_{W}\|_{\mathrm{op}} is the Hessian operator norm at the signpost. At d𝒯​(x,n∗)=τ∗d_{\mathcal{T}}(x,n^{*})=\tau^{*}, the marginal cost of using the cache equals the marginal cost of full inference.

Proof.

The expected total cost when using a Level-2 expert with routing radius τ\tau is:

Cost⁡(τ)=Chit⋅P⁡(hit)⏟cheap path+Cfull⋅P⁡(miss)⏟expensive path+λ⋅𝔼⁡[error2∣hit]⏟error cost.\mathrm{Cost}(\tau)=\underbrace{C_{\mathrm{hit}}\cdot P(\text{hit})}_{\text{cheap path}}+\underbrace{C_{\mathrm{full}}\cdot P(\text{miss})}_{\text{expensive path}}+\underbrace{\lambda\cdot\mathbb{E}[\text{error}^{2}\mid\text{hit}]}_{\text{error cost}}.

Error cost model. By Theorem 4, for a hit at query xx with divergence embedding r=‖E⁡(xd¯+1)−E⁡(nd¯+1∗)‖r=\|E(x_{\bar{d}+1})-E(n^{*}_{\bar{d}+1})\|, the squared error is ≤14​‖HW‖op2⋅r4\leq\frac{1}{4}\|H_{W}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\cdot r^{4}. We model the expected squared rr for queries routed to the expert as increasing with τ\tau: concretely, for the local approximation 𝔼⁡[r2∣hit]≈(Λ⁡(W)​CE)2⋅τ2\mathbb{E}[r^{2}\mid\text{hit}]\approx(\Lambda(W)C_{E})^{2}\cdot\tau^{2}, which holds when the conditional distribution of rr given d𝒯​(x,n∗)≤τd_{\mathcal{T}}(x,n^{*})\leq\tau concentrates at r≈Λ⁡(W)​CE⋅τr\approx\Lambda(W)C_{E}\cdot\tau (the Lipschitz-propagated trie distance). Under this approximation:

𝔼⁡[error2∣hit]≈14​‖HW‖op2⋅(Λ⁡(W)​CE)2⋅τ2.\mathbb{E}[\text{error}^{2}\mid\text{hit}]\;\approx\;\tfrac{1}{4}\|H_{W}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\cdot(\Lambda(W)C_{E})^{2}\cdot\tau^{2}.

Miss probability model. P⁡(miss)=1−Pℳ​(ℬ⁡(n∗,τ))≈1−c​τP(\text{miss})=1-P_{\mathcal{M}}(\mathcal{B}(n^{*},\tau))\approx 1-c\tau for small τ\tau, where c=limτ→0Pℳ​(ℬ⁡(n∗,τ))/τc=\lim_{\tau\to 0}P_{\mathcal{M}}(\mathcal{B}(n^{*},\tau))/\tau is the local PℳP_{\mathcal{M}}-density in trie metric space.

Optimization. Differentiating Cost⁡(τ)\mathrm{Cost}(\tau) and setting to zero:

−(Cfull−Chit)⋅c+λ2∥HW∥op2⋅(Λ(W)CE)2⋅τ=0,-(C_{\mathrm{full}}-C_{\mathrm{hit}})\cdot c+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|H_{W}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\cdot(\Lambda(W)C_{E})^{2}\cdot\tau=0,

giving τ∗=2​(Cfull−Chit)⋅c/(λ⋅‖HW‖op2​Λ​(W)2​CE2)\tau^{*}=2(C_{\mathrm{full}}-C_{\mathrm{hit}})\cdot c/(\lambda\cdot\|H_{W}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\Lambda(W)^{2}C_{E}^{2}). For the canonical case c=1c=1 this simplifies to the stated formula. ∎

Remark 3 (Too Close for Missiles, Switching to Guns).

The Abort-and-Replan Threshold theorem formalizes the fighter pilot’s abort signal. When d𝒯​(x,n∗)>τ∗d_{\mathcal{T}}(x,n^{*})>\tau^{*}, the input is “too far from the signpost”—the cached expert cannot engage. The system aborts the cache-hit path and switches to the base model (“guns”). The abort condition is a single comparison, O⁡(1)O(1), requiring no model queries. τ∗\tau^{*} is precomputed from WW at model-load time, exactly as the minimum missile engagement range is computed during mission planning.

5.5 LAWS as a Generalization

Theorem 10 (LAWS Generalizes MoE and KV Caching).
  1. (a)

    MoE as a special case. Any MoE model with KK experts and router RR is equivalent to a LAWS system with KK fixed Level-1 experts and a PLT trie of depth 1.

  2. (b)

    KV caching as a special case. Standard KV prefix caching is equivalent to LAWS with τ∗=−log⁡Pℳ​(n∗)\tau^{*}=-\log P_{\mathcal{M}}(n^{*}) (prefix match) and f=identityf=\mathrm{identity} (return cached activations verbatim).

  3. (c)

    Strict containment. LAWS with online expert creation is not representable as any fixed-KK MoE or as exact KV caching.

Proof.

(a) Given MoE experts {e1,…,eK}\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{K}\}, construct a PLT trie with KK leaf nodes n1,…,nKn_{1},\ldots,n_{K} at depth 1. Assign trie edge weights P⁡(nk∣root)=𝔼x​[R​(x)k]P(n_{k}\mid\text{root})=\mathbb{E}_{x}[R(x)_{k}] (the expected routing probability of expert kk). Set fnk=ekf_{n_{k}}=e_{k} and τ∗​(nk)=∞\tau^{*}(n_{k})=\infty (each expert covers its entire Voronoi cell in the abstract expert space). Define the parameter extractor ϕ\phi so that expert eke_{k} is selected whenever R​(x)kR(x)_{k} is largest (i.e., the MoE router outcome determines which expert is selected). Since the PLT trie here indexes expert labels rather than linguistic token prefixes, and a​u∗=∞au^{*}=\infty ensures every query is a cache hit, LAWS inference replicates MoE top-1 routing exactly. For top-k′k^{\prime} sparse MoE, use k′k^{\prime} routing balls with a​u∗=∞au^{*}=\infty and weighted averaging. ✓\checkmark

(b) Standard KV prefix caching stores activations for exact token prefixes. A LAWS expert with n∗=n^{*}= prefix, f=f= identity (return stored KV), τ∗=−log⁡Pℳ​(n∗)\tau^{*}=-\log P_{\mathcal{M}}(n^{*}) (matching all xx for which n∗n^{*} is a prefix), is exactly a KV cache entry under any-match routing. ✓\checkmark

(c) For strict containment: LAWS creates experts online from cache misses, so |ℒ||\mathcal{L}| is unbounded and grows with NN. Any fixed-KK MoE has |ℒ|=K<∞|\mathcal{L}|=K<\infty fixed at training. As N→∞N\to\infty, |ℒLAWS|→∞>K|\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LAWS}}|\to\infty>K. LAWS cannot be represented by a fixed-KK MoE. The same argument applies to KV caching with a finite cache size. ✓\checkmark ∎

Corollary 5 (LAWS is Strictly More Expressive).

For any fixed-KK MoE or finite KV cache, there exists a query distribution PP and a query count N∗​(P,K)N^{*}(P,K) such that for all N>N∗​(P,K)N>N^{*}(P,K), LAWS achieves strictly higher expected hit rate than the MoE or KV cache.

Proof.

By Theorem 6, LAWS’s hit rate is non-decreasing and converges to PP-coverage of the expert library. For a fixed-KK MoE or cache, hit rate is bounded by ∑k=1KP⁡(ℬ⁡(nk∗,τk∗))\sum_{k=1}^{K}P(\mathcal{B}(n^{*}_{k},\tau^{*}_{k})), which is fixed. LAWS’s coverage grows with NN, eventually exceeding the fixed system’s coverage for any PP with entropy >0>0. ∎

5.6 Automatic Symbolic Vocabulary

Theorem 11 (Automatic Symbolic Vocabulary).

Let 𝒱ε​(ℳ)\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{M}) denote the set of PLT trie nodes nn with probability mass Pℳ​(n)≥εP_{\mathcal{M}}(n)\geq\varepsilon. 𝒱ε​(ℳ)\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{M}) constitutes a symbolic vocabulary with the following provable properties:

  1. (a)

    Coverage: 𝒱ε\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon} contains at most ⌊1/ε⌋\lfloor 1/\varepsilon\rfloor nodes (count bound). For the probability covered by 𝒱ε\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon}: by Markov’s inequality applied to the surprisal −log2⁡Pℳ​(x)-\log_{2}P_{\mathcal{M}}(x),

    Pℳ​(𝒱ε)=Pℳ​(Pℳ​(x)≥ε)≥ 1−H⁡(Pℳ)log2⁡(1/ε),P_{\mathcal{M}}(\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon})=P_{\mathcal{M}}\!\bigl(P_{\mathcal{M}}(x)\geq\varepsilon\bigr)\;\geq\;1-\frac{H(P_{\mathcal{M}})}{\log_{2}(1/\varepsilon)},

    where H⁡(Pℳ)H(P_{\mathcal{M}}) is the Shannon entropy. In particular, for ε=2−H/δ\varepsilon=2^{-H/\delta}, the vocabulary 𝒱ε\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon} covers at least 1−δ1-\delta of the probability mass.

  2. (b)

    Compositionality: for any n,n′∈𝒱εn,n^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon}, their longest common prefix n∧n′n\wedge n^{\prime} is also in 𝒱ε\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon} whenever Pℳ​(n∧n′)≥εP_{\mathcal{M}}(n\wedge n^{\prime})\geq\varepsilon.

  3. (c)

    Graded similarity: the trie metric d𝒯d_{\mathcal{T}} is a well-defined pseudometric on 𝒱ε\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon}, giving graded rather than binary match/no-match.

  4. (d)

    Self-certification: validity of any symbolic approximation using n∈𝒱εn\in\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon} as a signpost is certified by Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W) without human authorship or additional inference.

  5. (e)

    Automatic discovery: 𝒱ε​(ℳ)\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{M}) is derived entirely from WW and PℳP_{\mathcal{M}}—no human intervention is required.

Proof.

(a) Let ℱε⊆𝒱ε\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon} be the frontier: the maximal (antichain) elements of 𝒱ε\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon}, i.e., nodes with Pℳ​(n)≥εP_{\mathcal{M}}(n)\geq\varepsilon that have no proper-prefix ancestor also in 𝒱ε\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon}. The frontier nodes are disjoint (no sequence matches two incomparable trie paths), so ∑n∈ℱεPℳ​(n)≤1\sum_{n\in\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}}P_{\mathcal{M}}(n)\leq 1, giving |ℱε|≤⌊1/ε⌋|\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}|\leq\lfloor 1/\varepsilon\rfloor. The full 𝒱ε\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon} may be larger (containing all ancestors of frontier nodes), but the count bound applies to the frontier.

For the coverage bound: by Markov’s inequality applied to the random variable −log2⁡Pℳ​(x)-\log_{2}P_{\mathcal{M}}(x) (the surprisal), whose expectation is H⁡(Pℳ)H(P_{\mathcal{M}}):

Pℳ​(−log2⁡Pℳ​(x)≥log2⁡(1/ε))≤H⁡(Pℳ)log2⁡(1/ε).P_{\mathcal{M}}\!\bigl(-\log_{2}P_{\mathcal{M}}(x)\geq\log_{2}(1/\varepsilon)\bigr)\;\leq\;\frac{H(P_{\mathcal{M}})}{\log_{2}(1/\varepsilon)}.

The complementary event −log2⁡Pℳ​(x)<log2⁡(1/ε)-\log_{2}P_{\mathcal{M}}(x)<\log_{2}(1/\varepsilon) is exactly Pℳ​(x)>εP_{\mathcal{M}}(x)>\varepsilon, i.e., x∈𝒱εx\in\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon}. Therefore Pℳ​(𝒱ε)≥1−H/log2⁡(1/ε)P_{\mathcal{M}}(\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon})\geq 1-H/\log_{2}(1/\varepsilon). Setting ε=2−H/δ\varepsilon=2^{-H/\delta} gives coverage ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta. ✓\checkmark

(b) The PLT trie is a prefix tree: every prefix of a sequence in the trie is also in the trie. If n∧n′n\wedge n^{\prime} has Pℳ≥εP_{\mathcal{M}}\geq\varepsilon, it is by definition in 𝒱ε\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon}.

(c) The trie metric satisfies: d⁡(s,s)=−log⁡P⁡(s)≥0d(s,s)=-\log P(s)\geq 0, d⁡(s,s′)=d⁡(s′,s)d(s,s^{\prime})=d(s^{\prime},s) (symmetry), and the ultrametric inequality d⁡(s,s′′)≤max⁡(d⁡(s,s′),d⁡(s′,s′′))d(s,s^{\prime\prime})\leq\max(d(s,s^{\prime}),d(s^{\prime},s^{\prime\prime})); see [15]. Since d⁡(s,s)=0d(s,s)=0 only when P⁡(s)=1P(s)=1 (a degenerate case), d𝒯d_{\mathcal{T}} is technically a pseudoultrametric rather than a true metric, giving graded rather than binary similarity.

(d) Theorem 3.

(e) The construction of 𝒱ε\mathcal{V}_{\varepsilon} uses only WW (to compute PℳP_{\mathcal{M}} and run inference to collect samples) and the PLT trie structure, both derived from WW without human authorship. ∎

6 Parametrized Experts: Construction and Theory

6.1 Pattern Recognition

Given a trie node n∗n^{*} with NminN_{\min} samples, the pattern recognition step fits the cheapest function from a candidate class hierarchy.

Proposition 1 (PAC Bounds for Pattern Recognition).

For a trie node n∗n^{*} with samples {(xi,yi)}i=1N\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} drawn from the subtree distribution, and a hypothesis class ℱ\mathcal{F} with fat-shattering dimension dfatd_{\mathrm{fat}}, the pattern recognition step selects f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} satisfying ‖y−f⁡(ϕ⁡(x))‖≤εfit\|y-f(\phi(x))\|\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}} for all samples. With probability ≥1−δPAC\geq 1-\delta_{\mathrm{PAC}}, this ff also satisfies the bound on unseen inputs in the subtree, given N≥NminN\geq N_{\min} where:

Nmin​(εfit,δPAC,dfat)=O⁡(dfatεfit2​log⁡dfatδPAC).N_{\min}(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}},\delta_{\mathrm{PAC}},d_{\mathrm{fat}})=O\!\left(\frac{d_{\mathrm{fat}}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}^{2}}\log\frac{d_{\mathrm{fat}}}{\delta_{\mathrm{PAC}}}\right).

For primitive classes: linear (dfat=O⁡(k⋅dout)d_{\mathrm{fat}}=O(k\cdot d_{\mathrm{out}}), where kk is the parameter dimension), lookup (dfat=O⁡(|table|)d_{\mathrm{fat}}=O(|\mathrm{table}|)), and template (dfat=O⁡(template length)d_{\mathrm{fat}}=O(\text{template length})).

Proof.

Standard uniform convergence bound for real-valued function classes (Bartlett and Mendelson [4]). For regression with ℓ2\ell^{2} loss, the fat-shattering dimension at scale εfit\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}} governs the sample complexity. The VC dimension bounds follow from the standard results for each function class. ∎

6.2 Small MLP Approximation

Theorem 12 (MLP Fitting Bound).

For any continuous function f:ℝk→ℝdoutf:\mathbb{R}^{k}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}} on a compact domain DD (the parameter space restricted to the validity ball) with Lipschitz constant Cf≤Λ⁡(W)C_{f}\leq\Lambda(W), there exists a ReLU MLP with at most:

Nneurons=O⁡(k⋅dout⋅(Cf/ε)k)N_{\mathrm{neurons}}=O\!\left(k\cdot d_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot(C_{f}/\varepsilon)^{k}\right)

neurons that approximates ff uniformly to within ε\varepsilon on DD. Here dout=|V|d_{\mathrm{out}}=|V| when approximating full logit output, or dout=dmodeld_{\mathrm{out}}=d_{\mathrm{model}} when approximating an intermediate hidden state.

Proof.

By the Barron approximation theorem [1]: for functions with bounded spectral norm in kk input dimensions, a single-hidden-layer network with mm neurons achieves L2L^{2} error O⁡(Cf2/m)O(C_{f}^{2}/m), giving m=O⁡(Cf2/ε2)m=O(C_{f}^{2}/\varepsilon^{2}) for L2L^{2} approximation. For uniform (L∞L^{\infty}) approximation on a compact domain, the Cybenko theorem and subsequent quantitative refinements (e.g., Yarotsky [23]) give O⁡((Cf/ε)k)O((C_{f}/\varepsilon)^{k}) neurons for depth-O⁡(log⁡(1/ε))O(\log(1/\varepsilon)) networks. Multiplying by doutd_{\mathrm{out}} output dimensions gives the stated bound. ∎

Corollary 6 (Small MLP Size for Low-Dimensional Parameters).

For a trie node where kk (the number of high-entropy parameter positions, per Theorem 5) is small (e.g., k=3k=3 for binary search, k=2k=2 for arithmetic), the MLP has O⁡(dout⋅(Cf/ε)3)O(d_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot(C_{f}/\varepsilon)^{3}) neurons. For dout=dmodel=4096d_{\mathrm{out}}=d_{\mathrm{model}}=4096 (caching the final hidden state rather than full vocabulary logits, which is typical for chained LAWS inference), Cf=0.1C_{f}=0.1 (normalized), ε=0.01\varepsilon=0.01: Nneurons≈4096⋅103≈4×106N_{\mathrm{neurons}}\approx 4096\cdot 10^{3}\approx 4\times 10^{6}. This MLP has <50<50 MB footprint—evaluable in microseconds on a GPU versus milliseconds for a full forward pass.

6.3 Cross-Architecture Portability

Theorem 13 (Cross-Architecture Expert Portability).

A LAWS expert (n∗,f,ϕ,τ∗,εfit)(n^{*},f,\phi,\tau^{*},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}) constructed from base model ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} is valid for a different base model ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2} if:

maxx∈ℬ⁡(n∗,τ∗)⁡‖FW2​(x)−f⁡(ϕ⁡(x))‖≤δ.\max_{x\in\mathcal{B}(n^{*},\tau^{*})}\|F_{W_{2}}(x)-f(\phi(x))\|\leq\delta.

This condition is testable by sampling NN inputs from ℬ⁡(n∗,τ∗)\mathcal{B}(n^{*},\tau^{*}) and checking the bound; with confidence 1−δPAC1-\delta_{\mathrm{PAC}}, PAC bounds from Proposition 1 apply. The routing radius for ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2} is τ2∗=(δ−εfit(2)−2​Λ​(W2)⋅CE)/(Λ⁡(W2)⋅CE)\tau^{*}_{2}=(\delta-\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{fit}}-2\,\Lambda(W_{2})\cdot C_{E})/(\Lambda(W_{2})\cdot C_{E}), where εfit(2)=‖FW2​(n∗)−f⁡(ϕ⁡(n∗))‖\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{fit}}=\|F_{W_{2}}(n^{*})-f(\phi(n^{*}))\| is the fitting error re-measured on ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}.

Proof.

The expert ff represents a computation, not a specific model. Its validity for ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2} depends only on whether FW2F_{W_{2}} approximates ff on the domain, independently of how ff was constructed. Testing against ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}’s outputs is an independent PAC learning problem with the same sample complexity bounds. ∎

7 The Cinderella Effect

7.1 The Problem

A natural question in any attention-sparsification scheme is whether a token with small attention weight at layer ℓ\ell might become important at a later layer ℓ′>ℓ\ell^{\prime}>\ell—the Cinderella effect: a token plucked from obscurity by a later layer’s attention mechanism, its small initial weight amplified into a large influence on the final output.

Definition 5 (Cinderella Event).

A Cinderella event at layer ℓ\ell, position jj occurs when: ai​j(ℓ)≤εa^{(\ell)}_{ij}\leq\varepsilon (small attention weight at layer ℓ\ell) but the counterfactual output difference from zeroing this entry satisfies: ‖Δ​Outputi(L)‖>α\|\Delta\mathrm{Output}^{(L)}_{i}\|>\alpha (large influence on final output) for some significance threshold α≫ε\alpha\gg\varepsilon.

7.2 The Cascade Bound

Theorem 14 (Cinderella Cascade Bound).

If token jj has attention weight ai​j(ℓ)≤εa^{(\ell)}_{ij}\leq\varepsilon at layer ℓ\ell, then:

  1. (a)

    The worst-case cascade satisfies:

    ‖Δ​Outputi(L)‖≤ε⋅‖𝐯j(ℓ)‖⋅∏m=ℓL−1κ(m).\|\Delta\mathrm{Output}^{(L)}_{i}\|\leq\varepsilon\cdot\|\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}_{j}\|\cdot\prod_{m=\ell}^{L-1}\kappa^{(m)}.
  2. (b)

    A Cinderella event (large final impact despite small initial weight) can only occur if token jj’s surprisal satisfies:

    hj≥hCin=dhead⋅log2⁡(α/ε)4​κ2​CE2​ln⁡2⋅‖q‖2​‖k‖2,h_{j}\geq h_{\mathrm{Cin}}=\frac{d_{\mathrm{head}}\cdot\log^{2}(\alpha/\varepsilon)}{4\kappa^{2}C_{E}^{2}\ln 2\cdot\|q\|^{2}\|k\|^{2}},

    where κ=maxℓ⁡κ(ℓ)\kappa=\max_{\ell}\kappa^{(\ell)} is the maximum per-layer coupling constant from Theorem 1, CEC_{E} is the embedding diameter, and dheadd_{\mathrm{head}} is the per-head dimension. (The log2\log^{2} arises from squaring the logit-increase condition 2​κ​CE​hj​ln⁡2​‖q‖​‖k‖/dhead≥log⁡(α/ε)2\kappa C_{E}\sqrt{h_{j}\ln 2}\|q\|\|k\|/\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{head}}}\geq\log(\alpha/\varepsilon) when solving for hjh_{j}.)

  3. (c)

    For tokens with hj<hCinh_{j}<h_{\mathrm{Cin}} (low-surprisal tokens), the Cinderella event cannot occur. These tokens are safely sparsifiable.

Proof.

Part (a). Zeroing attention entry ai​j(ℓ)a^{(\ell)}_{ij} introduces error ei(ℓ)=ai​j(ℓ)⋅𝐯j(ℓ)e^{(\ell)}_{i}=a^{(\ell)}_{ij}\cdot\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}_{j}, with ‖ei(ℓ)‖≤ε​‖𝐯j(ℓ)‖\|e^{(\ell)}_{i}\|\leq\varepsilon\|\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}_{j}\|. This error enters the residual stream and propagates through layers ℓ+1,…,L\ell+1,\ldots,L. Each layer mm is κ(m)\kappa^{(m)}-Lipschitz (Lemma 1), so:

‖ei(m+1)‖≤κ(m)​‖ei(m)‖.\|e^{(m+1)}_{i}\|\leq\kappa^{(m)}\|e^{(m)}_{i}\|.

Iterating from ℓ\ell to LL: ‖Δ​Outputi‖≤ε​‖𝐯j(ℓ)‖​∏m=ℓL−1κ(m)\|\Delta\mathrm{Output}_{i}\|\leq\varepsilon\|\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}_{j}\|\prod_{m=\ell}^{L-1}\kappa^{(m)}. ✓\checkmark

Part (b). For a Cinderella event, the attention weight of jj at layer ℓ+1\ell+1 must increase substantially: ai​j(ℓ+1)≥α≫εa^{(\ell+1)}_{ij}\geq\alpha\gg\varepsilon. The logit for token jj at layer ℓ+1\ell+1, relative to what it would be if token jj’s embedding had been replaced by its context-predicted mean (the counterfactual baseline), changes by:

Δ​logitj=1dhead​(𝐪i(ℓ+1)⋅Δ​𝐤j(ℓ+1)+Δ​𝐪i(ℓ+1)⋅𝐤j(ℓ+1)),\Delta\mathrm{logit}_{j}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{head}}}}\bigl(\mathbf{q}^{(\ell+1)}_{i}\cdot\Delta\mathbf{k}^{(\ell+1)}_{j}+\Delta\mathbf{q}^{(\ell+1)}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{k}^{(\ell+1)}_{j}\bigr),

where Δ​𝐤\Delta\mathbf{k} and Δ​𝐪\Delta\mathbf{q} are the deviations of the key/query vectors from this baseline. By Theorem 1 and the surprisal-bounded embedding variance of [17], a token with per-token surprisal hjh_{j} has expected embedding deviation ≤CE​hj​ln⁡2\leq C_{E}\sqrt{h_{j}\ln 2} from its context-predicted mean (using the updated variance-entropy bound), which propagates through the κ\kappa-Lipschitz layer map to give:

‖Δ​𝐤j(ℓ+1)‖,‖Δ​𝐪i(ℓ+1)‖≤κ⋅CE⋅hj​ln⁡2,\|\Delta\mathbf{k}^{(\ell+1)}_{j}\|,\|\Delta\mathbf{q}^{(\ell+1)}_{i}\|\leq\kappa\cdot C_{E}\cdot\sqrt{h_{j}\ln 2},

so |Δ​logitj|≤2​κ​CE​hj​ln⁡2⋅‖q‖​‖k‖/dhead|\Delta\mathrm{logit}_{j}|\leq 2\kappa C_{E}\sqrt{h_{j}\ln 2}\cdot\|q\|\|k\|/\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{head}}}. For the attention weight to increase from ε\varepsilon to α\alpha, the logit must increase by at least log⁡(α/ε)\log(\alpha/\varepsilon) (to leading order, assuming other attention scores are approximately unchanged). Setting 2​κ​CE​hj​ln⁡2​‖q‖​‖k‖/dhead≥log⁡(α/ε)2\kappa C_{E}\sqrt{h_{j}\ln 2}\|q\|\|k\|/\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{head}}}\geq\log(\alpha/\varepsilon) and solving for hjh_{j} gives hj≥hCinh_{j}\geq h_{\mathrm{Cin}}.

Part (c). The contrapositive: hj<hCin⇒h_{j}<h_{\mathrm{Cin}}\Rightarrow Cinderella event cannot occur (logit increase is too small to bring jj from ε\varepsilon-weight to α\alpha-weight). ✓\checkmark ∎

Corollary 7 (Shannon Overflow Set).

Define the Shannon overflow set 𝒪ε={j:hj≥hCin}\mathcal{O}_{\varepsilon}=\{j:h_{j}\geq h_{\mathrm{Cin}}\}. Tokens in 𝒪ε\mathcal{O}_{\varepsilon} may exhibit Cinderella events and must be retained in full-precision computation. Tokens not in 𝒪ε\mathcal{O}_{\varepsilon} are safe to sparsify or cache-hit. The expected size of 𝒪ε\mathcal{O}_{\varepsilon} is:

𝔼⁡[|𝒪ε|]=n⋅Pℳ​(hj≥hCin)≤n⋅log2⁡PP⁡(ℳ)hCin,\mathbb{E}[|\mathcal{O}_{\varepsilon}|]=n\cdot P_{\mathcal{M}}(h_{j}\geq h_{\mathrm{Cin}})\leq n\cdot\frac{\log_{2}\mathrm{PP}(\mathcal{M})}{h_{\mathrm{Cin}}},

which approaches zero as hCin→∞h_{\mathrm{Cin}}\to\infty (larger threshold, smaller overflow set).

Proof.

Markov’s inequality applied to the surprisal random variable: P⁡(hj≥hCin)≤𝔼⁡[hj]/hCin=log2⁡PP⁡(ℳ)/hCinP(h_{j}\geq h_{\mathrm{Cin}})\leq\mathbb{E}[h_{j}]/h_{\mathrm{Cin}}=\log_{2}\mathrm{PP}(\mathcal{M})/h_{\mathrm{Cin}}. ∎

8 Robotics and Fleet Learning

8.1 The Robotics Challenge

Modern robot controllers—whether model-based (MPC, trajectory optimization) or learned (diffusion policy, transformer-based visuomotor)—face a fundamental tension: they must be accurate (avoiding catastrophic failure) yet fast (100+ Hz control loops). Full trajectory optimization or neural network inference at each control timestep is expensive. Current approaches use one of: (1) hard-coded motion primitives (inflexible, brittle to novel objects); (2) offline-trained policies (cannot generalize to new environments without retraining); or (3) online adaptation (expensive, requires backpropagation at runtime).

LAWS offers a fourth path: automatic discovery and certification of motion primitives from actual task executions, growing richer with fleet experience, downloadable as compact updates.

8.2 LAWS for Robotic Motor Programs

Definition 6 (Robotic LAWS Expert).

A robotic LAWS expert e=(ntask∗,π,ϕ,τ∗,εfit)e=(n^{*}_{\mathrm{task}},\pi,\phi,\tau^{*},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}) where:

  • •

    ntask∗n^{*}_{\mathrm{task}} is a PLT trie node over task descriptions (natural language or sensor embedding);

  • •

    π:ℝk→𝒜T\pi:\mathbb{R}^{k}\to\mathcal{A}^{T} is a motor program mapping task parameters to an action sequence;

  • •

    ϕ\phi extracts task parameters (object pose, target location, mass, friction coefficient);

  • •

    τ∗\tau^{*} is the validity radius derived from the controller’s Lipschitz constant Λ⁡(Wctrl)\Lambda(W_{\mathrm{ctrl}}).

8.3 State of the Art and LAWS Improvements

Current state-of-the-art robotic policies include: Diffusion Policy [6] (denoising diffusion for visuomotor control), RT-2 [5] (vision-language-action models), and π0\pi_{0} [3] (flow-matching generalist policies). These achieve impressive generalization but require full neural network inference at every control step: typically 50–200 ms per action, limiting real-time control frequency.

Proposition 2 (LAWS Speedup for Repetitive Tasks).

For a task distribution PtaskP_{\mathrm{task}} with entropy HtaskH_{\mathrm{task}} and a LAWS expert library with hit rate HnH_{n}, the expected control step latency is:

𝔼⁡[TLAWS]=Hn⋅Texpert+(1−Hn)⋅Tfull,\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathrm{LAWS}}]=H_{n}\cdot T_{\mathrm{expert}}+(1-H_{n})\cdot T_{\mathrm{full}},

where Texpert≪TfullT_{\mathrm{expert}}\ll T_{\mathrm{full}}. For a robot performing repetitive household tasks (object manipulation, item retrieval, fixture interaction) with Hn≥0.9H_{n}\geq 0.9 (achievable after sufficient deployment), 𝔼⁡[TLAWS]≈Texpert\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathrm{LAWS}}]\approx T_{\mathrm{expert}}, enabling order-of-magnitude latency reduction.

8.4 Fleet Learning Theorems

Theorem 15 (Fleet Learning Lower Bound).

Consider KK LAWS-equipped robotic units, each performing MM tasks per day, all contributing observations to a shared central LAWS library. Under a stationary task distribution PtaskP_{\mathrm{task}}:

  1. (a)

    After DD deployment days, the shared library has at most O⁡(2H⁡(Ptask)​log⁡(K​M​D))O(2^{H(P_{\mathrm{task}})}\log(KMD)) experts.

  2. (b)

    The fleet hit rate HK,DH_{K,D} is non-decreasing in DD (by Theorem 6) and converges to full coverage as K​M​D→∞KMD\to\infty: since O⁡(2H​log⁡(K​M​D))O(2^{H}\log(KMD)) distinct heavy trie nodes are visited and each expert creation strictly increases the hit rate, HK,D→1H_{K,D}\to 1 for any distribution with finite entropy HH.

  3. (c)

    The fleet achieves the same hit rate as a single unit in time DK≈D1/KD_{K}\approx D_{1}/K, i.e., convergence is Ω⁡(K)\Omega(K) faster than single-unit deployment.

Proof.

Part (a). By Theorem 7, each unit alone creates O⁡(2H​log⁡(M​D))O(2^{H}\log(MD)) experts. With KK units sharing a library, total queries are K​M​DKMD. Applying Theorem 7 with N=K​M​DN=KMD: O⁡(2H​log⁡(K​M​D))O(2^{H}\log(KMD)) experts (valid when K​M​D≤Nmin⋅2HKMD\leq N_{\min}\cdot 2^{H}; for larger K​M​DKMD all heavy nodes are covered and HK,D=1H_{K,D}=1, satisfying the bound since min⁡(1,⋅)=1\min(1,\cdot)=1), where H=H⁡(Ptask)H=H(P_{\mathrm{task}}). ✓\checkmark

Part (b). By Theorem 6, each expert creation strictly increases HK,DH_{K,D}. By part (a), O⁡(2H​log⁡(K​M​D))O(2^{H}\log(KMD)) experts are created, covering an increasing fraction of the input distribution. Since H⁡(Ptask)H(P_{\mathrm{task}}) is finite, all O⁡(2H)O(2^{H}) heavy trie nodes are eventually visited, and HK,D→1H_{K,D}\to 1 as K​M​D→∞KMD\to\infty. ✓\checkmark

Part (c). From part (b), both a single unit and the KK-unit fleet converge to hit rate HK,D→1H_{K,D}\to 1. The fleet converges KK times faster because it generates K​MKM queries per day (versus MM for a single unit), discovering the same O⁡(2H)O(2^{H}) heavy trie nodes in 1/K1/K the time. The improvement factor is D1/DK=KD_{1}/D_{K}=K, giving the stated Ω⁡(K)\Omega(K) convergence speedup. ✓\checkmark ∎

Corollary 8 (Network Effect).

The fleet learning benefit is superlinear in KK for small KK and approaches KK-linear for large KK (the log correction vanishes as M→∞M\to\infty). This formalizes the network effect of experience: each additional unit contributes its workload to the shared library, benefiting all other units. A fleet of 1,000 robots converges to high hit rate roughly 1,000 times faster than a single robot.

8.5 Over-the-Air (OTA) Expert Updates

Theorem 16 (OTA Update Bandwidth Bound).

The incremental LAWS expert library update covering the period [t,t+Δ​t][t,t+\Delta t] (representing Δ​N=K​M​Δ​t\Delta N=KM\Delta t new observations) has description length:

ℒΔ​t=O⁡(2H⁡(Ptask)⋅log⁡(Δ​N)⋅Bexpert)​ bits,\mathcal{L}_{\Delta t}=O\!\left(2^{H(P_{\mathrm{task}})}\cdot\log(\Delta N)\cdot B_{\mathrm{expert}}\right)\text{ bits},

where BexpertB_{\mathrm{expert}} is the description length of a single expert (Theorem 17 below). For Δ​t=24\Delta t=24 hours, K=1000K=1000 units, M=100M=100 tasks/unit/day (Δ​N=105\Delta N=10^{5}):

ℒΔ​t=O⁡(2H⋅log⁡(105)⋅Bexpert)≈O⁡(2H⋅17⋅Bexpert).\mathcal{L}_{\Delta t}=O\!\left(2^{H}\cdot\log(10^{5})\cdot B_{\mathrm{expert}}\right)\approx O(2^{H}\cdot 17\cdot B_{\mathrm{expert}}).

For Bexpert≈50B_{\mathrm{expert}}\approx 50 KB (small MLP), H≈10H\approx 10 bits (2H=10242^{H}=1024): ℒ24​h≈870\mathcal{L}_{24\mathrm{h}}\approx 870 MB per day for the full fleet update. Individual robot updates are ≈870\approx 870 KB per day per unit—feasible on any connected device.

Proof.

The number of new experts in period Δ​t\Delta t is O⁡(2H​log⁡(Δ​N))O(2^{H}\log(\Delta N)) by Theorem 7. Each expert has description length BexpertB_{\mathrm{expert}}. Total bits: O⁡(2H​log⁡(Δ​N)⋅Bexpert)O(2^{H}\log(\Delta N)\cdot B_{\mathrm{expert}}). Substituting Δ​N=K​M​Δ​t\Delta N=KM\Delta t gives the bound. Per-unit update: if units have approximately disjoint workload domains (each unit specializes in different task types), then on average 1/K1/K of the new experts are relevant to any one unit, giving per-unit download O⁡(2H​log⁡(Δ​N)⋅Bexpert/K)O(2^{H}\log(\Delta N)\cdot B_{\mathrm{expert}}/K) bits. In the homogeneous case (all units share the same task distribution), each unit downloads all new experts and the per-unit cost equals the fleet total. ∎

Theorem 17 (Expert Description Length).

For a trie node n∗n^{*} with kk parameter dimensions and validity radius τ∗\tau^{*}, the minimum description length of a LAWS expert achieving output error ≤ε\leq\varepsilon is:

B⁡(n∗,ε)=Ω⁡(k⋅dout⋅log⁡τ∗ε)​ bits.B(n^{*},\varepsilon)=\Omega\!\left(k\cdot d_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot\log\frac{\tau^{*}}{\varepsilon}\right)\text{ bits}.

A small MLP expert (Theorem 12) requires O⁡(k⋅dout⋅(Cf/ε)k⋅32)O(k\cdot d_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot(C_{f}/\varepsilon)^{k}\cdot 32) bits (at fp32), which is exponentially larger in kk than this lower bound. The gap reflects the curse of dimensionality for general Lipschitz approximation; for specific structured function classes (linear, lookup, template), the description length matches the lower bound to within polylogarithmic factors.

Proof.

Lower bound: to represent a Lipschitz function f:ℝk→ℝdoutf:\mathbb{R}^{k}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}} to uniform accuracy ε\varepsilon over a parameter ball of radius τ∗\tau^{*}, one must distinguish Ω⁡((τ∗/ε)k)\Omega((\tau^{*}/\varepsilon)^{k}) cells in the kk-dimensional input space (by a standard covering argument) and specify doutd_{\mathrm{out}} output values per cell to precision ε\varepsilon. The total description length is therefore Ω⁡((τ∗/ε)k⋅dout⋅log⁡(1/ε))\Omega((\tau^{*}/\varepsilon)^{k}\cdot d_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)) bits.

The stated bound B⁡(n∗,ε)=Ω⁡(k⋅dout⋅log⁡(τ∗/ε))B(n^{*},\varepsilon)=\Omega(k\cdot d_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot\log(\tau^{*}/\varepsilon)) is a weaker lower bound obtained by taking the log\log of the cell count: log⁡((τ∗/ε)k)=k​log⁡(τ∗/ε)\log((\tau^{*}/\varepsilon)^{k})=k\log(\tau^{*}/\varepsilon), so any description of the cell index alone requires Ω⁡(k​log⁡(τ∗/ε))\Omega(k\log(\tau^{*}/\varepsilon)) bits, giving Ω⁡(k⋅dout⋅log⁡(τ∗/ε))\Omega(k\cdot d_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot\log(\tau^{*}/\varepsilon)) bits total for doutd_{\mathrm{out}} output dimensions. The MLP construction in Theorem 12 achieves O⁡(k⋅dout⋅(Cf/ε)k)⋅32O(k\cdot d_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot(C_{f}/\varepsilon)^{k})\cdot 32 bits (at fp32); the gap between this upper bound and the lower bound reflects the exponential dependence on kk inherent in approximating kk-dimensional Lipschitz functions. ∎

Remark 4 (Differential Privacy).

The OTA update can incorporate differential privacy [9] by adding calibrated Gaussian noise to the expert parameters before uploading. The privacy cost is bounded by the description length: an expert update of BB bits can achieve (εDP,δDP)(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DP}},\delta_{\mathrm{DP}})-differential privacy with noise scale σ=2​B​ln⁡(1.25/δDP)/εDP\sigma=\sqrt{2B\ln(1.25/\delta_{\mathrm{DP}})}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DP}}. For B=50B=50 KB, δ=10−5\delta=10^{-5}, εDP=1\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DP}}=1: σ≈0.03\sigma\approx 0.03, adding 3% noise to expert parameters—within the fitting error tolerance for most experts.

9 Comparison to Prior Work

9.1 LAWS vs. KV Caching

Standard transformer KV caching [18, 13] stores key-value vectors for exact token prefixes, enabling reuse across requests sharing a common prefix. The companion paper [17] extended this to approximate prefix matching via the PLT trie metric, and proved that sequential KV compression can exceed TurboQuant’s per-vector Shannon limit by exploiting the sequential structure of token streams.

LAWS extends both in several fundamental ways:

  • •

    LAWS is not restricted to KV vectors—it caches any intermediate computation or final output.

  • •

    LAWS experts are parametrized: they compute a function of the input’s variable parameters, not a fixed stored value.

  • •

    LAWS validity domains are formally certified by Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W); standard KV caching has no validity theory.

  • •

    LAWS’s library grows with deployment; KV caches have finite size with eviction policies.

Formally, Theorem 10(b) shows KV caching is the degenerate case τ∗=0\tau^{*}=0, f=identityf=\mathrm{identity}. LAWS with τ∗>0\tau^{*}>0 and nontrivial ff is strictly more powerful.

9.2 LAWS vs. Mixture of Experts

Standard MoE [20, 10, 8] maintains a fixed pool of KK expert sub-networks, trained jointly with the router. Fast Feed-Forward Networks (FFF) [2] replace the router with a binary tree, achieving O⁡(log⁡K)O(\log K) routing. Symbolic MoE [21] routes to skill-based expert models selected by an LLM router.

The key distinctions from LAWS:

  • •

    Fixed vs. growing: all MoE variants fix KK at training. LAWS’s |ℒ||\mathcal{L}| grows unboundedly with deployment.

  • •

    Training vs. inference-time: MoE experts are trained jointly with the base model; LAWS experts are created at inference time from observed outputs.

  • •

    No validity guarantee: no MoE variant provides a formal guarantee that any expert is correct on any given input. LAWS provides ‖LAWS⁡(x)−FW​(x)‖≤δ\|\mathrm{LAWS}(x)-F_{W}(x)\|\leq\delta for all inputs in certified validity domains.

  • •

    Routing basis: MoE routing is learned; LAWS routing uses the PLT trie metric derived from WW, requiring no routing training.

Theorem 10(a) shows MoE is the LAWS special case with fixed ℒ\mathcal{L} and depth-1 trie.

9.3 LAWS vs. Cyc

Cyc [14] encoded common-sense knowledge as explicit logical axioms, requiring approximately 47,000 person-years of manual knowledge entry. Its knowledge base is static, brittle (fails outside authored rules), and provides no formal guarantee of correctness.

LAWS shares Cyc’s goal (a reusable knowledge library for fast symbolic-style inference) but differs fundamentally: its vocabulary is discovered automatically from the training distribution (Theorem 11), grows with deployment, provides formal validity certificates, and requires no human authorship. The comparison:

Property Cyc LAWS
Knowledge source Human-authored Automatic from WW
Update mechanism Manual Online from queries
Validity guarantee None Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W)-certified
Graceful degradation No Yes (εfit+2​Λ​CE\varepsilon_{\mathrm{fit}}+2\Lambda C_{E} uniform bound)
Generalization beyond rules None Jacobian correction
Human labor required ≫104\gg 10^{4} person-years None

9.4 LAWS vs. Wolfram Alpha

Wolfram Alpha [22] curates computational knowledge in specific domains (mathematics, science, geography) and provides exact symbolic computation within those domains. Outside the curated domain, it fails entirely.

LAWS differs in: (1) domain coverage is automatic (whatever the base model learned); (2) experts in Level-3 (primitive function) are exactly the kind of computation Wolfram Alpha performs—but discovered automatically; (3) generalization beyond exact matches is formal (Jacobian correction); (4) Wolfram Alpha cannot grow its knowledge base from user queries.

The deepest distinction: Wolfram Alpha’s knowledge is organized by human experts according to mathematical structure. LAWS’s knowledge is organized by probability structure—the trie metric d𝒯d_{\mathcal{T}} is the natural metric for a system that learned from language, not the human-designed ontology that organizes Wolfram’s knowledge base.

10 Conjectures and Open Problems

Conjecture 1 (Effective Lipschitz Concentration).

For a transformer FWF_{W} trained to near-zero cross-entropy loss on a corpus with entropy HH, the effective Lipschitz constant on inputs drawn from PℳP_{\mathcal{M}} concentrates well below the worst-case Λ⁡(W)\Lambda(W):

Λeff=𝔼x∼Pℳ[supx′:‖E⁡(x′)−E⁡(x)‖≤ε‖FW​(x′)−FW​(x)‖‖E⁡(x′)−E⁡(x)‖]≪Λ(W).\Lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{\mathcal{M}}}\!\left[\sup_{x^{\prime}:\|E(x^{\prime})-E(x)\|\leq\varepsilon}\frac{\|F_{W}(x^{\prime})-F_{W}(x)\|}{\|E(x^{\prime})-E(x)\|}\right]\;\ll\;\Lambda(W).
